opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the fundamental tension is about timelines. If you're designing a chip, you're making bets that won't land in silicon for maybe two or three years, and then that chip has to stay useful for several more years after that. Meanwhile, on the model side, attention has been evolving pretty quickly. A few years ago everyone was doing standard multi-head attention. Then we moved to multi-query and grouped-query attention to shrink the KV cache for inference. Now you see things like multi-head latent attention, sliding window and local-global hybrids, various sparse attention patterns, and of course hybrid architectures that mix attention with state space model layers or linear attention. Each of these has a pretty different computational profile.

And that matters a lot for hardware, because the bottleneck shifts depending on the variant. Standard attention during decoding is very memory-bandwidth bound, since you're reading this big KV cache for every token you generate. If you compress the KV cache, like with grouped-query or latent attention, the arithmetic intensity goes up and suddenly you're closer to being compute bound. If you move to state space models or linear attention, you have a fixed-size recurrent state, so the memory picture changes completely, and you care much more about things like scan operations or chunked matrix multiplies. So if a chip designer heavily specializes, say by building a lot of dedicated hardware around one specific attention pattern or picking a particular ratio of memory bandwidth to compute based on today's workloads, they risk optimizing for something that's no longer what people run by the time the chip ships.

That's part of why I think GPUs have been so durable. They're specialized enough, with tensor cores for matrix multiplies, but programmable enough that when someone comes up with a new attention variant, people like us can write a new kernel and get good utilization within weeks. For a more specialized accelerator, the risk is that the workload moves out from under you. So the challenge for chip designers is figuring out what's actually stable. Matrix multiplication is very stable; that's not going anywhere. But the exact shape of attention, the memory access patterns, how much state you carry around during inference, those are still very much in flux. You want to bet on the invariants and keep flexibility everywhere else.

There's also a co-design aspect going the other way. Model architects increasingly pick designs that run well on existing hardware, which is partly why some ideas win and others don't. So the hardware and the architectures kind of shape each other, and if you're building a new chip you're trying to predict where that feedback loop will end up, which is genuinely hard.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is there's this really tight coupling between the hardware and the algorithms, and the timelines are just mismatched. If you're designing a chip, you're making bets today on what workloads are going to look like two, three, maybe four years from now, because that's how long it takes to tape out, validate, ramp production, get it into data centers. And the algorithms side moves way faster than that. We see new attention variants every few months.

So concretely, a lot of chip designers looked at transformers around 2020, 2021, and said, okay, the workload is matrix multiplication, let's build enormous amounts of matmul throughput, maybe some fixed-function units for softmax, that kind of thing. And that's a reasonable bet. But then the question is, what happens when the attention mechanism itself changes? Like, if you go to something like linear attention or state space models or any of these recurrent-style formulations, the computational structure is different. You have these scan operations, you have different memory access patterns, the ratio of compute to memory bandwidth shifts. And if your chip was built around the assumption that it's all dense matmul with very specific shapes, you might find that it's sitting there underutilized.

Even within standard attention, things like how you do the KV cache, whether you're doing grouped query attention, multi-query attention, the shapes of the matrices change, the amount of memory traffic changes. With FlashAttention, a big part of what we did was restructure the computation to be aware of the memory hierarchy, and that was for GPUs. If a chip has a different memory hierarchy, you have to rethink that.

So I think the challenge is really about how much flexibility you build in versus how much you specialize. The more you specialize, the better your efficiency on today's workload, but the more exposed you are if the workload shifts. And honestly, I think the workload will keep shifting. That's kind of the nature of this field right now. So I'd rather see hardware that's fast at a broad class of operations and lets the software people adapt on top, rather than hardware that's hyper-optimized for one specific formulation of attention that might not be what we're using in two years.

astra-6.text:
The challenge is that hardware takes much longer to design than it takes us to change the model architecture. If you’re designing a chip, you’re making bets about what workloads will look like several years from now. But researchers can change how attention works in a matter of months.

For example, you might build specialized hardware assuming that attention always constructs this big matrix of interactions between tokens. Then people find ways to compute attention without materializing that matrix, or they move toward sparse attention or architectures with a different memory pattern. The computation your chip was optimized for might no longer be the bottleneck.

So there’s a tension between specialization and flexibility. Specialization can give you really good efficiency, but you want to specialize around things that will remain useful—like matrix multiplication—while retaining enough programmability to support changes in how those operations are organized and how data moves through memory.

sol-6.1.text:
The challenge is that the architecture is still moving, while designing a chip takes a long time. If you build hardware that’s very specialized for one form of attention, by the time the chip comes out, people might be using a different form of attention—or a model that replaces attention altogether.

And those changes can really affect what the hardware needs to do. Standard attention has large matrix multiplications, but other approaches might introduce different memory access patterns or recurrent updates. A chip that’s great at one isn’t necessarily great at the other.

So there’s this tradeoff: specialization can give you better efficiency, but you need enough flexibility to keep up with the algorithms. That makes hardware and algorithm co-design really important.
